In the Odyssey, a bard sings of how this goddess's husband, the smith god, caught her in bed with Ares in a net he had forged.
This goddess hid the baby Adonis in a chest and left him with Persephone, then fought her for him until Zeus split his year into thirds.
This Greek goddess of love and beauty was said to have been born from sea foam, coming ashore near the island of Cyprus.

aphrodite.writerNotes: 'Venus' is not added as an alias: she is the Roman counterpart, not another name, and Venus is already an answer in the bank (the planet). A player who types Venus will be marked wrong.

clues.text: This writer's first wife, Hadley, lost a suitcase filled with his manuscripts at the Gare de Lyon train station in Paris in 1922.
This author survived two plane crashes in Uganda within about a day in 1954, then got to read newspaper obituaries that had reported him dead.
About 50 cats, many with six toes, roam this writer's former Key West home; the first was said to be a gift from a visiting sea captain.
This American author of 'The Old Man and the Sea' and 'A Farewell to Arms' won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1954.

ernest-hemingway.writerNotes: Sources differ on the gap between the two crashes (12 hours to two days), so clue 2 says 'within about a day'. The cat count changes over time (sources give 40 to 60); Ripley's says about 50. Hemingway's son Patrick has disputed that today's cats descend from the first one, so clue 3 avoids claiming descent.

clues.text: In 1924 the champions taking this trophy to their victory party set it on a roadside curb during car trouble, drove off without it, and later found it still there.
The bowl on top of this trophy originally cost ten guineas, and every 13 years the oldest band of names is removed to make room for new winners.
Engravers have misspelled team names on this trophy, carving 'BQSTQN' for the Boston Bruins in 1972 and 'Leaes' for the Toronto Maple Leafs in 1963.
This trophy, the oldest awarded to a pro sports team in North America, goes to the NHL champions, and each winning player gets to keep it for a day.

stanley-cup.writerNotes: Accounts of the 1924 Montreal Canadiens incident disagree on whether it was a flat tire or a stalled car being pushed uphill, so clue 1 says only 'car trouble'. The day-with-the-Cup tradition dates from 1995.

clues.text: The figures in this collection were once brightly painted, but much of the color can flake off in as little as four minutes once the surrounding mud is cleared away.
Bronze weapons buried with this collection survived about 2,200 years with little decay; a 2019 study credited the soil, not a chromium coating long thought to be the secret.
Farmers digging a well in Shaanxi province in 1974 found the first pieces of this collection, buried about 1.5 km east of an emperor's tomb mound.
This collection of life-size clay soldiers, horses and chariots was buried near Xi'an to guard China's first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, in the afterlife.
This painter, sent to Hawaii in 1939 to make art for a pineapple company's ads, came back with a papaya tree—a rival's fruit—and painted a pineapple only once one was shipped to her studio.
Of Cerro Pedernal, a flat-topped mountain she painted again and again, this artist said: 'God told me if I painted it enough, I could have it.'
Her husband, the photographer Alfred Stieglitz, made more than 350 portraits of this painter before he gave up photography in 1937.
This American modernist won international fame for her paintings of flowers and of the New Mexico desert.

georgia-okeeffe.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia says she painted the pineapple only after the company sent a plant to her New York studio; artnet says papaya was a rival company's product.

clues.text: Ancient writers linked this creature to the poisonous plant aconite, saying the foam it spilled when dragged into daylight either created the plant or poisoned it.
The poet Hesiod gave this monster fifty heads and Pindar gave it a hundred, though most ancient art shows far fewer.
In Dante's Inferno, this creature guards the third circle of Hell, where it claws and flays the souls of the gluttons.
This three-headed dog guarded the gates of the Greek underworld, and dragging it up to the surface was one of Heracles' labours—in most tellings, the last.

cerberus.writerNotes: Clue 1: Herodorus and Euphorion say aconite grew from its bile; Ovid says its foam poisoned aconite growing nearby, so the clue says 'sprang from, or was poisoned by'. Clue 4: Apollodorus makes it the twelfth labour, Diodorus the eleventh, hence 'in most tellings'.

clues.text: This writer walked with a limp for the rest of his life after his 26-year-old nephew shot him in the leg with a pistol in 1886.
One of this novelist's books, rejected by his publisher and long thought lost, was found by his great-grandson in 1989 and finally published in 1994.
UNESCO has ranked this author the world's second most-translated writer since 1979, behind Agatha Christie and ahead of Shakespeare.
This French author wrote 'Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas' and 'Around the World in Eighty Days'.

jules-verne.writerNotes: Clue 2 is Paris in the Twentieth Century. Clue 3: Wikipedia cites UNESCO (2013) for 'second most-translated author in the world since 1979'.

clues.text: This athlete's 13th individual Olympic title, won in 2016, broke a record held for more than 2,000 years by Leonidas of Rhodes, an ancient Greek runner.
This athlete won one 2008 Olympic final by a hundredth of a second, and video analysis upheld the result after Serbia protested.
In another 2008 final, this athlete's goggles filled with water and he said he couldn't see for the last 100 meters, yet he still set a world record.
This swimmer from Baltimore won eight golds at the 2008 Beijing Games and 23 Olympic golds in all.

michael-phelps.writerNotes: Clue 1: Leonidas won 12 individual titles, the last in 152 BC; 2016 - 152 BC gives the 2,168 years most outlets used. His events were foot races, including one run in armour. Clue 2 is the 100m butterfly over Milorad Čavić.

clues.text: This singer's camper caught fire on a 1965 fishing trip, starting a blaze that burned 508 acres of a California forest and drove off 49 of its 53 endangered condors.
This singer said that as an Air Force Morse code operator in West Germany he copied the first news of Stalin's death in 1953, though some old colleagues doubted it.
This singer duets with Bob Dylan on the opening track of Dylan's 1969 album Nashville Skyline and won a Grammy for writing that album's liner notes.
Known as the Man in Black, this country singer married June Carter and sang 'Folsom Prison Blues'.

johnny-cash.writerNotes: Clue 2 is hedged: Cash's 1997 autobiography says 'I copied the first news of Stalin's death'; Steve Turner's biography quotes a former colleague calling it nonsense. Clue 1: the fire was in Los Padres National Forest; Wikipedia gives 508 acres and 49 of 53 condors.

clues.text: This painter was a part-time bartender when he discovered Bill Alexander's TV painting show; Alexander later told The New York Times, 'He betrayed me.'
This artist spent about 20 years in the U.S. Air Force, including a stint at a base in Alaska, and decided never to raise his voice again once he left.
A 2014 FiveThirtyEight count of 381 paintings this artist made on air found trees in 91% of them, clouds in 44% and mountains in 39%.
This soft-spoken, permed host of PBS's 'The Joy of Painting' assured viewers that there are no mistakes, just 'happy accidents.'
This creature was the emblem on the sleeve badge of Britain's wartime airborne troops, and a Normandy canal bridge they seized by glider in June 1944 was renamed after it weeks later.
In one telling, this creature sprang from the blood of Medusa's neck as Perseus beheaded her, together with its brother Chrysaor.
The Hippocrene, a spring on Mount Helicon sacred to the Muses whose name means 'horse's fountain', was said to gush up where this creature struck the ground with its hoof.
The hero Bellerophon tamed this winged horse of Greek myth with a golden bridle given to him by Athena.

pegasus.writerNotes: Clues 2-4 are sourced to Wikipedia only.

clues.text: The first model of this gadget had an extra headphone jack and a 'hotline' button that switched on a built-in microphone so two listeners could talk over the music.
In 1982 Woodbridge, New Jersey, made it illegal even to cross the street while wearing this gadget's headphones.
This gadget was first sold in the UK as the 'Stowaway', in the US as the 'Sound-about' and in Australia and Sweden as the 'Freestyle'.
Sony launched this portable cassette player in 1979 and sold about 220 million cassette models before ending production in 2010.

walkman.writerNotes: Clue 2: Woodbridge has a township council; sources disagree on who pushed the ban, so the clue names the township, not a person.

clues.text: This water sport's regulars swallow up to ten times as much seawater as sea swimmers, and a 2018 Exeter study found them about three times as likely to carry drug-resistant E. coli.
Lieutenant James King, completing Captain Cook's journals after Cook was killed in 1779, became the first person to write about this pastime in Hawaii.
At the 2024 Paris Olympics this sport was held in Tahiti, about 15,700 km away — the farthest any Olympic medal event has been staged from its host city.
Hawaiian Olympic swimmer Duke Kahanamoku spread this sport, riding ocean waves while standing on a board, to Australia and the United States.

surfing.writerNotes: Clue 1: coverage of the Exeter 'Beach Bums' study mostly says three times as likely; one report says four times. Clue 3: outlets give 15,600-15,730 km; 'about 15,700 km' covers them.

clues.text: This singer weighed 13.5 pounds at birth, and the forceps used to deliver him scarred his left cheek and neck and damaged his left eardrum for life.
In the 1940s this singer's publicist, George Evans, paid girls $5 each to scream at strategic spots in his audiences.
The night after this singer died in May 1998, the Empire State Building glowed blue in his honor.
This Hoboken-born crooner led the Rat Pack in Las Vegas and recorded 'My Way' and 'New York, New York'.
